section.title: The Catch of Fish and the Call of Levi
section.sectionRationale: Having announced His mission, Jesus now begins to gather those who will carry it. A miraculous catch of fish exposes Simon Peter's sin and calls him to catch men; a leper is cleansed by a touch; a paralytic is forgiven and healed, revealing the Son of Man's authority to forgive; and a tax collector named Levi leaves his booth to follow. Around a table of sinners Jesus declares that He came not for the righteous but to call sinners to repentance, and the parables of the patch and the wineskins signal that something wholly new has arrived.
section.thesis: Jesus calls sinners, not the self-sufficient, drawing fishermen, lepers, the paralyzed, and tax collectors to Himself, forgiving sins and healing bodies with divine authority, and announcing that the new thing He brings cannot be sewn onto the old.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the miraculous catch and the call of Simon, James, and John; the cleansing of a leper; the forgiveness and healing of a paralytic; the call of Levi and the meal with sinners; and the parables of the patch and the wineskins.

units.label: Put out into deep water
units.note: from now on you will catch men

verses.text: On one occasion, while Jesus was standing by the Lake of Gennesaret with the crowd pressing in on Him to hear the word of God,
He saw two boats at the edge of the lake. The fishermen had left them and were washing their nets.
Jesus got into the boat belonging to Simon and asked him to put out a little from shore. And sitting down, He taught the people from the boat.
When Jesus had finished speaking, He said to Simon, “Put out into deep water and let down your nets for a catch.”
“Master,” Simon replied, “we have worked hard all night without catching anything. But because You say so, I will let down the nets.”
When they had done so, they caught such a large number of fish that their nets began to tear.
So they signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them, and they came and filled both boats so full that they began to sink.
When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees. “Go away from me, Lord,” he said, “for I am a sinful man.”
For he and his companions were astonished at the catch of fish they had taken,
and so were his partners James and John, the sons of Zebedee. “Do not be afraid,” Jesus said to Simon. “From now on you will catch men.”
And when they had brought their boats ashore, they left everything and {{akoloutheo|followed}} Him.
While Jesus was in one of the towns, a man came along who was covered with leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he fell facedown and begged Him, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.”
Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!” And immediately the leprosy left him.
“Do not tell anyone,” Jesus instructed him. “But go, show yourself to the priest and present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing, as a testimony to them.”
But the news about Jesus spread all the more, and great crowds came to hear Him and to be healed of their sicknesses.
Yet He frequently withdrew to the wilderness to pray.

units.label: Your sins are forgiven
units.note: the Son of Man's authority to forgive

verses.text: One day Jesus was teaching, and the Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there. People had come from Jerusalem and from every village of Galilee and Judea, and the power of the Lord was present for Him to heal the sick.
Just then some men came carrying a paralyzed man on a mat. They tried to bring him inside to set him before Jesus,
but they could not find a way through the crowd. So they went up on the roof and lowered him on his mat through the tiles into the middle of the crowd, right in front of Jesus.
When Jesus saw their faith, He said, “Friend, your sins are {{aphiemi|forgiven}}.”
But the scribes and Pharisees began thinking to themselves, “Who is this man who speaks blasphemy? Who can forgive sins but God alone?”
Knowing what they were thinking, Jesus replied, “Why are you thinking these things in your hearts?
Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’?
But so that you may know that the Son of Man has {{exousia|authority}} on the earth to forgive sins...” He said to the paralytic, “I tell you, get up, pick up your mat, and go home.”
And immediately the man stood up before them, took what he had been lying on, and went home glorifying God.
Everyone was taken with amazement and glorified God. They were filled with awe and said, “We have seen remarkable things today.”

units.label: The call of Levi
units.note: I have not come to call the righteous but sinners

verses.text: After this, Jesus went out and saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax booth. “{{akoloutheo|Follow Me}},” He told him,
and Levi got up, left everything, and followed Him.
Then Levi hosted a great banquet for Jesus at his house. A large crowd of tax collectors was there, along with others who were eating with them.
But the Pharisees and their scribes complained to Jesus’ disciples, “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?”
Jesus answered, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.
I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to {{metanoia|repentance}}.”

units.label: New wine, new wineskins
units.note: the bridegroom and the newness of the kingdom

verses.text: Then they said to Him, “John’s disciples and those of the Pharisees frequently fast and pray, but Yours keep on eating and drinking.”
Jesus replied, “Can you make the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them?
But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.”

He also told them a parable: “No one tears a piece of cloth from a new garment and sews it on an old one. If he does, he will tear the new garment as well, and the patch from the new will not match the old.
And no one pours new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins, the wine will spill, and the wineskins will be ruined.
Instead, new wine is poured into new wineskins.
And no one after drinking old wine wants new, for he says, ‘The old is better.’”

akoloutheo.gloss: To follow, to come after as a disciple. It means more than walking behind; it is attaching one's whole life to a master. The fishermen and Levi akoloutheo Jesus by leaving everything, the pattern of true discipleship throughout the Gospel.

aphiemi.gloss: To let go, release, forgive, send away. It is the verb behind the noun for forgiveness. When Jesus tells the paralytic his sins are aphiemi, forgiven, He does what the scribes rightly say only God can do, and then heals the man to prove His authority to do it.

exousia.gloss: Authority, the rightful power to act. Jesus claims that the Son of Man has exousia on earth to forgive sins, and He backs the claim with a visible healing, showing that His authority reaches into the invisible realm of guilt and pardon.

metanoia.gloss: A change of mind that turns the whole life around; repentance. Jesus says He came to call sinners to metanoia, not to affirm the self-righteous. The tax collectors and sinners at Levi's table are exactly the people His call is for.

basic.context: After announcing His mission, Jesus begins to gather followers. He tells the tired fisherman Simon to let down his nets, and the overwhelming catch drives Simon to his knees as a sinner; Jesus calls him to catch men. Jesus cleanses a leper with a touch, forgives and heals a paralytic lowered through a roof, and calls a tax collector named Levi, then feasts with sinners. When criticized, He says He came for the sick, not the healthy, and tells parables of a patch and wineskins to show that His kingdom is something new.
basic.hermeneutics: Read these scenes together as a portrait of who Jesus calls and how. The common thread is grace to the unlikely: sinful fishermen, an untouchable leper, a helpless paralytic, a despised tax collector. The forgiveness of the paralytic is the theological center, where Jesus claims divine authority. The wineskins parable interprets the whole: the new wine of the kingdom cannot simply be poured into the old forms.
basic.originalLanguages: The fishermen and Levi akoloutheo Jesus, follow Him, by leaving everything. Jesus tells the paralytic his sins are aphiemi, forgiven, doing what only God can do, and proves He has exousia, authority, to forgive by healing him. And He declares He came to call sinners to metanoia, repentance, the turning that the proud think they do not need.
basic.typology: The cleansing of the leper by touch, without Jesus being defiled, points to the One who takes our uncleanness and makes us clean. The forgiveness of the paralytic reveals the Son of Man of Daniel 7, given authority and dominion. The bridegroom image casts Jesus as the long-promised husband of His people, whose presence is cause for joy, not fasting.
basic.christ: Jesus is Lord over creation, commanding the fish; He is holy, so that Simon feels his sin in His presence; He is the compassionate healer who touches the untouchable; He is the Son of Man with authority to forgive; and He is the friend of sinners and the bridegroom of His people. In every scene He draws the unworthy to Himself and makes them His own.
basic.god: God's power is present in Jesus to heal and, more wonderfully, to forgive, the prerogative the scribes rightly reserve to God alone. God calls not the self-righteous but sinners, welcoming tax collectors to the table. And God is doing a genuinely new thing in Jesus that cannot be contained by the old religious forms.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 6 shows the same holy fear before God that Simon feels. Leviticus 13 and 14 lie behind the leper's cleansing and the priestly testimony. Daniel 7:13-14 names the Son of Man given authority. 1 Timothy 1:15 sums it up: Christ came to save sinners.
basic.oneStory: The Savior who announced good news to the poor now gathers a people of the unlikely. He calls sinful fishermen, cleanses a leper, forgives a paralytic with divine authority, and seats a tax collector at His table, declaring that He came for sinners. The new wine of His kingdom is bursting the old skins; the age of the bridegroom has arrived, and He is drawing the guilty and the outcast into the joy of following Him.

context.literary:
Luke 5 is a chain of five scenes, each one drawing a different kind of person toward Jesus, and the chain tightens as it goes. The first two scenes, the fishing boat and the leper, are stories of encounter, and the crowd is a backdrop. From verse 17 the mood changes. Pharisees and teachers of the law appear in the story for the first time in Luke, and the three scenes that follow, the paralytic, Levi's banquet and the question about fasting, are each framed by an objection. Together with the two Sabbath disputes of Luke 6:1-11, they make a block of five controversies. The movement is from wonder to suspicion to plot, a rhythm that Luke 6:11 completes when the opponents begin to discuss what they might do to Jesus.

The scenes are arranged by a rising ladder of need. Simon confesses that he is a sinful man. The leper is ritually unclean. The paralytic is helpless and, as Jesus sees it, guilty. Levi is socially despised. Each man is further from the respectable centre, and each is met by Jesus' action: a command, a touch, a word of forgiveness, an invitation to follow. The final scene turns the question from persons to principle, and the images of cloth and wine ask what kind of new thing this is.

There is also a pattern of speech and answer. Three times a person speaks and Jesus responds directly: Simon, 'Go away from me, Lord,' verse 8, the leper, 'Lord, if You are willing,' verse 12, and the opponents' unspoken thought in verse 21, which Jesus answers in verse 22 as though they had said it aloud. Luke likes the detail that Jesus knows what is in the heart.

The closing parable has a surprise. Luke alone adds the line that a person who has drunk old wine says, 'The old is better,' verse 39. It is a rueful observation that ends the chapter on the note of resistance. The reader is left to feel the pull of the familiar, which is the real obstacle to the kingdom.
context.historical:
Luke calls the Sea of Galilee a lake, 'the Lake of Gennesaret,' verse 1, which is the term a Greek writer would use for an inland body of water. The shore was lined with fishing villages, and fishing was a trade carried out by crews, often family partnerships. Simon, Andrew, James and John worked together, and Luke calls James and John Simon's 'partners,' verse 10, a word that carries the sense of shared enterprise. As fishermen on that lake still know, much of the work was done at night, and a catch in deep water after a night of nothing was against ordinary experience. Simon's tired reply in verse 5 is the voice of a professional.

Leprosy in the Bible is a broad term for a range of skin diseases, and the law of Moses treated the person as ritually unclean. The leper had to live apart, wear torn clothes and cry 'Unclean, unclean!' Leviticus 13:45-46, and recovery had to be examined and certified by a priest with prescribed offerings, Leviticus 14:2-4. Jesus' instruction in verse 14 to go to the priest follows that law, and the phrase 'as a testimony to them' means that the priestly verdict would be public evidence that something had happened. The ban on touching was also a social wall. To touch a leper was, in the law's terms, to share in uncleanness, and Jesus' reaching out His hand is a deliberate crossing of that wall.

The paralytic's friends carry him to a house crowded to the doors. Houses in Galilee often had flat roofs reached by an outside stair, and Luke says they let him down 'through the tiles,' while Mark describes digging through the roof. The two details are not in conflict, since a roof of tiles and beams could be opened. The Pharisees and teachers of the law who have come 'from Jerusalem and from every village of Galilee and Judea,' verse 17, are an official delegation. Their reaction to a claim to forgive sins was grounded in the law's own view that only God can pardon, and they were guarding what they believed to be a sacred boundary.

Tax collectors in Galilee under Herod Antipas worked for the state or its contractors, collecting tolls and duties on goods that moved along the roads. They were held to be collaborators with an occupying power and had a reputation for taking more than was due. John the Baptist had to tell them to 'collect no more than you are authorized,' Luke 3:13. Levi sitting at his booth was a man whom respectable Jews avoided, and a meal at his table was a social statement. Fasting, finally, was a mark of devotion. The law commanded one fast, on the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 16:29, but groups of the devout added more, and the Pharisee of Luke 18:12 says 'I fast twice a week.' The question in verse 33 comes from people who thought piety had to look a certain way.
context.canonical:
Each scene reaches into the Old Testament and then out into the rest of Luke and the New Testament. The call of Simon follows the pattern of the call of Isaiah. Isaiah sees the LORD and cries, 'Woe is me, for I am ruined,' Isaiah 6:5, and is cleansed and commissioned. Simon sees what Jesus can do and falls at His knees, saying that he is a sinful man, and is commissioned in turn. The detail of fish and men has a prophetic background as well. Jeremiah 16:16 speaks of God sending for many fishermen and then many hunters, a picture of gathering that in Jeremiah's context is about judgment. Ezekiel's vision of the river from the temple has fishermen standing along the shore, Ezekiel 47:10. Jesus takes the old image of the net and turns it toward a gathering for life.

Simon's story returns after the resurrection. In John 21 the same disciples fish all night and catch nothing, a figure on the shore tells them where to cast the net, the catch is more than they can haul, and Peter recognises 'It is the Lord!' and plunges in, John 21:3-7. The miracle in Luke 5 is the first act of a pattern that Jesus completes after Easter, in which Peter's calling is renewed.

The leper's cleansing is part of the list of signs Jesus gives to John's disciples, Luke 7:22, and Mark's parallel shows the same plea, 'If You are willing, You can make me clean,' Mark 1:40-42. The forgiveness of the paralytic touches the Psalms: 'He who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases,' Psalm 103:3, and Isaiah's promise of a Zion where the sick are gone and the people 'forgiven of iniquity,' Isaiah 33:24. The question 'Who can forgive sins but God alone?' rests on texts like Isaiah 43:25, where God says 'I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake,' and Exodus 34:6-7, which names forgiving iniquity as God's own character.

Levi's call and banquet are retold in Matthew 9:9-13, where Jesus adds 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' Hosea 6:6. The accusation that He welcomes sinners and eats with them returns in Luke 15:1-2 and 19:7, where the same grumbling meets Zacchaeus. And the bridegroom image draws on the prophets' picture of God as husband of His people, Isaiah 62:5, which John the Baptist takes up in John 3:29 and the New Testament carries to its end in the marriage of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke told Theophilus that he had set out an orderly account so that he might know the certainty of what he had been taught, Luke 1:1-4. In this chapter the certainty lies in who Jesus is and whom He calls. Luke wants his readers to see a Lord whose presence exposes sin and who then deals with it. Peter's cry shows the first reaction of anyone who sees Jesus truly, and Jesus' answer, 'Do not be afraid,' is the gospel in small.

Luke also wanted his readers to take the measure of the opposition. The leaders who sit and watch in verse 17 have the Scriptures, the temple and the traditions, and they are the ones who miss what is happening. It is a warning to readers who think of themselves as established in faith. The people who come are the ones who know that they cannot help themselves. The paralytic is carried by friends, the leper begs, and Levi is called away from his work.

The chapter is also meant to explain to Luke's later readers why the church looks the way it does. A community that includes tax collectors and sinners and does not fast on the old pattern might seem to have lost its way. Luke shows that the form of this community is determined by the presence of the Bridegroom, and the closing parables explain why the new life cannot be stitched onto the old garment. The message was pressing for Gentile readers, who might wonder whether they had to adopt the old forms first.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what Jesus did and said on particular occasions, not rules for the church to copy mechanically. It does not tell every believer to leave a trade at once and follow Him, as Simon and Levi did. Jesus' call to those men was a particular summons, and Luke 14:33 and Acts show that others served Him from their homes and trades. What every follower is called to is the same willingness to put Jesus first and to hold possessions loosely.

Nor does the account promise that every sickness will be healed as the leper's and the paralytic's were. Luke presents these as signs of the Messiah's authority and the nearness of the kingdom. And the link Jesus draws between the paralytic's forgiveness and his healing is not a rule that every illness has a particular sin behind it. Jesus corrects that assumption elsewhere, John 9:2-3.

What does carry over is the pattern of how Jesus treats people. He receives the unclean with a touch, the guilty with forgiveness and the despised with a seat at His table. The church is called to the same stance, joined with the same call to repentance. The Pharisees' complaint was not that Jesus ate with sinners but that He did so without condemning them, and the church is to follow Him in both. His comment on the new wine also bears on how believers handle their traditions: customs are good servants but cannot be allowed to contain what Christ has brought.

debates.question: In what sense does Jesus forgive sins in verse 20?

views.label: He declares what God has done, as a prophet
views.case: The verb 'are forgiven' is a perfect passive, a form that Jews often used to avoid naming God. Nathan told David, 'The LORD has taken away your sin,' 2 Samuel 12:13, without claiming to forgive himself. On this reading Jesus speaks as a prophet announcing God's pardon, and the scribes are wrong to call it blasphemy.

views.label: He forgives with His own authority
views.case: Verse 24 says that the Son of Man 'has authority on the earth to forgive sins.' The authority is His and it operates 'on the earth,' now. The scribes' question, 'Who can forgive sins but God alone?', is not corrected by Jesus. He accepts the premise and shows that the one who can heal with a word can also forgive. The reaction of the leaders, who understood Him to be claiming something divine, supports this reading.

views.label: He forgives as God's appointed representative
views.case: Some hold a middle position: He acts as the Son of Man of Daniel 7, the figure to whom God gives dominion, Daniel 7:13-14. The authority is real and personal but delegated by the Father, so that Jesus is neither a mere herald nor a rival to God.

debates.bearing: The text pushes toward the second and third views. Jesus does not deny the scribes' principle but answers it, and the sign He gives is meant to show that the authority is His own. At the least, Luke wants his readers to see that Jesus occupies a place that only God could occupy.

debates.question: What do the old garment and the old wineskins stand for?

views.label: The old covenant, replaced by the new
views.case: Jesus is bringing something so new that the old forms of Judaism cannot hold it. On this view the Law and the sacrificial system are the old garment, and the new covenant in His blood, Luke 22:20, is the new cloth. Hebrews 8:13 speaks of the first covenant as obsolete and aging.

views.label: Man-made traditions and expectations about piety
views.case: The context is a question about fasting and the practice of a particular kind of devotion. Jesus does not say that the law is old but that the expectations of the Pharisees' circle, and of John's disciples, cannot absorb the joy of His presence. On this reading Jesus' own words that He came to fulfil the Law, Matthew 5:17, forbid reading the parable as a rejection of Scripture.

views.label: A warning against mixing and against resisting
views.case: The parable has two edges. Verses 36 to 38 warn against patching the new onto the old, and verse 39 explains why people refuse the new. The point is not primarily about which system is better but about the human tendency to prefer what is familiar and to try to fit Jesus into what we already have.

debates.bearing: The second and third views are best supported by the immediate setting, while the first states what the New Testament later concludes about the old covenant, Galatians 3:23-25. Jesus does not reject the Scriptures, but His coming changes the shape of the life that responds to them.

study.originalLanguages:
When Peter answers in verse 5, he calls Jesus 'Master,' epistata, a word that only Luke uses among the Gospel writers, nearly always in the mouth of the disciples and always for one who has authority over a task. He then says that 'because You say so' he will let down the nets, which in Greek is literally 'at Your word,' epi to rhemati sou. The word is rhema, the spoken word, and it recalls Mary's reply to the angel, 'May it happen to me according to your word,' Luke 1:38. Peter's obedience to the word against his own experience is a small echo of her faith. After the catch the title changes. In verse 8 he addresses Jesus as 'Lord,' kyrie. He has begun by treating Jesus as a skilled teacher and ends by falling at His knees.

Peter calls himself 'a sinful man,' aner hamartolos, literally 'a man, a sinner.' The cry comes in response to the catch, not to any sermon on sin. It is the instinct of a person who has met power and holiness together. Jesus replies by speaking not about the sin but about the future: 'From now on you will catch men.' The verb is zogreo, from the words for 'alive' and 'to catch.' It means to take alive, and was used of capturing someone in battle rather than killing them. The only other New Testament use is in 2 Timothy 2:26, of people who are taken captive by the devil. A fisherman's catch dies, but the catch that Jesus promises is a catch into life.

Luke also says that in verse 11 they 'left everything,' using the participle aphentes, from aphiemi. That is the same verb as 'forgive' in verse 20, which means to let go, release or send away. In one chapter the verb describes the disciples releasing their boats and nets and Jesus releasing the paralytic from his sins. What the disciples let go of is small beside what is let go of for them.

In the paralytic story, 'Friend' in verse 20 is the Greek word anthrope, which is simply 'man.' The BSB softens it to 'Friend,' but the address is a plain, direct one that treats him as an individual. The words 'are forgiven' are in the perfect tense, apheontai, and stand for a completed action whose results continue. The man's sins have been dealt with and the matter is closed. The passive form leaves the agent unstated, and the debate about the passive is that Jesus then claims to be the agent in verse 24.

The title 'Son of Man' appears here for the first time in Luke, verse 24. It is a title that Jesus uses of Himself, and it recalls Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man receives dominion from the Ancient of Days. The sentence in verse 24 breaks off in the middle. Jesus begins 'But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority...' and then turns to the paralytic, so that the sentence is completed by the healing. The grammar is the action, and the command to rise is the end of the argument.

In verse 26 the crowd say they have seen 'remarkable things,' paradoxa, a word from which English gets 'paradox.' It means things beyond expectation. Luke adds that 'amazement,' ekstasis, took hold of everyone, a word that suggests being put outside oneself.

Finally, in verse 32 Jesus says that He came to call sinners 'to repentance.' The phrase eis metanoian is found in Luke's version only. Mark 2:17 and Matthew 9:13 in the BSB end with 'but sinners.' Luke adds the aim of the call. Jesus eats with sinners not to endorse them but to change them, and the call is to a changed mind and life. Jesus' reference to 'the righteous' is not an admission that anyone is righteous, since Luke has just shown that the supposedly righteous are the ones who do not see their need.

typology.type: The cleansing of the leper by touch, Leviticus 13 and 14
typology.fulfillment: Under the law, uncleanness passed by contact, and a person who touched what was unclean became unclean too, Leviticus 5:3. The leper had to live outside the camp, Leviticus 13:46. Jesus reverses the flow. He touches the man and instead of Jesus becoming unclean, the man becomes clean. The pattern is fulfilled in His whole work, for He 'took on our infirmities and carried our diseases,' Matthew 8:17, and 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. He also went outside the camp to bear reproach, Hebrews 13:12-13. The type has limits, since it speaks of one man's skin while Christ's cleansing deals with the whole person before God.

Daniel saw one like a son of man come with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and receive dominion, glory and a kingdom that would never be destroyed, Daniel 7:13-14. Jesus takes the title for Himself and uses it first for His authority on earth to forgive sins. The correspondence runs through Luke, as the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath, Luke 6:5, suffers, Luke 9:22, and comes in glory, Luke 21:27. The vision in Daniel speaks of heavenly authority. In Luke the authority begins in a crowded house in Capernaum with a paralysed man, and the cross is where it is exercised.

The prophets speak of the LORD as the husband of His people, rejoicing over her as a bridegroom over his bride, Isaiah 62:5. When Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom, He takes the place of the God of the covenant. John the Baptist calls himself the friend of the bridegroom and rejoices to hear His voice, John 3:29. The words 'the bridegroom will be taken from them' point ahead to the cross, and Paul describes Christ giving Himself up for His bride, Ephesians 5:25-27, until the marriage of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7. The image is a picture, and it breaks down if pressed: the church is not a bride because of her own beauty but because He washes her.

typology.type: The fishermen and the net, Jeremiah 16:16
typology.fulfillment: God had said through Jeremiah that He would send for many fishermen to catch His people, in a passage about gathering for judgment and return. Jesus takes the figure and puts a new purpose on it. The fishermen are His, the catch is 'men,' and the net draws them to life, as the verb zogreo implies. The scene is repeated after the resurrection in John 21, where the net is full and unbroken, and the church's mission is the continuing work of those who were first caught by Him. The type has a limit: Jeremiah's fishermen were part of a judgment, and Jesus' are sent into a harvest of grace.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by showing that He is Lord in every realm that touches human need. In the boat He is Lord of creation. At His word the fish of the lake are brought into the nets, and the Gospel of John says that all things were made through Him, John 1:3. The catch does not merely feed the fishermen; it shows who is in the boat. Peter's reaction is not to thank Jesus for a good day but to ask Him to go away, because he has seen Someone whose power is a holy power.

He is the holy one who draws near. Peter's 'Go away from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man' is the cry of Isaiah in the temple, and the answer is the same as it was to Isaiah, not departure but cleansing and a commission. Jesus' answer, 'Do not be afraid,' is the word that follows an encounter with God throughout Scripture. The fisherman is not sent away but sent out.

He is the one who touches the untouchable. The leper is covered with the disease, and Jesus reaches out His hand. The Law said that touching spreads uncleanness, and Jesus shows that His holiness spreads the other way. He asks the man to see the priest and to bring the offering Moses prescribed, so He neither despises the law nor makes Himself its slave. The 'I am willing' answers the man's 'if You are willing.' Jesus' will is the pivot of the whole Gospel. Later in Gethsemane the same Lord will pray, 'Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me. Yet not My will, but Yours be done,' Luke 22:42. The Lord who willingly cleanses the leper willingly goes to the cross.

He is the one who forgives sins and shows it. He sees the faith of the friends who carried the man and speaks first of the deeper need. The scribes' question is the right one, and the answer is that He is the Son of Man with authority. The sign of the healing is given 'so that you may know,' so that people will see that the invisible forgiveness is as real as the visible walking. Only the one who bears sin can pardon it, and the Gospel will show that He does so by His death. The word of pardon spoken in the house is paid for at Calvary.

He is the friend of sinners and the physician. Levi leaves his booth, and the next thing he does is give a banquet and bring his friends to meet Jesus, which is what a person does who has found something. Jesus' description of Himself as a doctor who has come for the sick is the same compassion that Paul states as a trustworthy saying: 'Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners,' 1 Timothy 1:15.

He is the bridegroom whose presence changes everything. The disciples do not fast because the joy of the wedding is here, and the hint that He will be taken away puts the cross beneath the feast. The new wine is the new covenant in His blood, Luke 22:20.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The tiles are not a code, the number of fish is not a message, and the nets are not a picture of the church's structure. What the passage supplies is a Lord who is holy, willing, authoritative and merciful, and the links above come from Luke's own details and the rest of the New Testament's use of the same texts.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as holy and near at once. Peter's terror in the boat is the right response to the presence of God in a person. Isaiah in the temple and Peter in the boat both found that to see the holiness of God was to see their own sin. And in both cases God does not leave them in that state. The holiness that exposes also cleanses and sends. In the leper's story the same holiness reaches out to touch, and God is shown to be a God who moves toward the unclean rather than away from them.

It shows God as the only one who forgives. The scribes' question, 'Who can forgive sins but God alone?', is correct. God's own self-revelation to Moses names Him as 'forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin,' Exodus 34:7, and Isaiah hears Him say, 'I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake,' Isaiah 43:25. Forgiveness is not a technicality but the heart of God's character, and it is not purchased by anything the sinner can bring. Micah's question, 'Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity?', Micah 7:18, is answered in the house at Capernaum in a way the people there did not expect.

It shows God's power joined to His mercy. The power of the Lord was present to heal, verse 17, and it was used on a man who could do nothing for himself. Power in the hands of the God of the Bible is never separated from compassion. The healing is also a gift to the friends who believed, since Jesus responds to their faith and does not require the paralytic to speak.

It shows God's initiative in calling. Jesus sees Levi at his booth and says two words, 'Follow Me.' The call is not a reward for good conduct, and the response, leaving everything, is the response of one who has been laid hold of. God does the calling and the changing, and His people follow because He has first called.

It shows that God is doing something new. The old forms, good as they were, were designed to point forward. The joy of the bridegroom, the new wine and the new garment point to a time when God dwells with His people in a way the law only anticipated. At the same time the passage is honest that the new is resisted. 'The old is better,' says the drinker of old wine, and the God of the Bible is patient with that instinct while still offering something better.

It reveals something of the Trinity. The power of the Lord is with Jesus, and the Son of Man exercises the authority that is God's own. He forgives as the Father forgives and acts in the Spirit's power, as Luke 4:18 has already said.

For worship, this means that God is not honoured by our pretending to be respectable. We come as Peter did, as sinners in the presence of the holy, and we hear the same words, 'Do not be afraid.' It also means celebrating. The feast at Levi's house, with a crowd of tax collectors and sinners at the table, is a picture of worship, since it is the joy of the forgiven in the presence of the one who forgave them.

crossReferences.note: The call of Isaiah and the call of Simon share a shape: a vision of holiness, a cry of unworthiness, cleansing and a commission. Isaiah says he is a man of unclean lips, Peter says he is a sinful man, and both are sent. Luke wants the reader to hear that Peter has met the same LORD whom Isaiah saw.

After the resurrection the same disciples fish all night and catch nothing until Jesus tells them where to cast the net. The catch is again too great to haul and Peter again responds to the Lord. The second miracle renews the first, and it prepares the way for Peter to be restored and sent to feed the flock.

The law of cleansing that Jesus tells the leper to follow. The priest examines the healed person and offers sacrifices on the day of cleansing, and the public rite restores the man to the community. Jesus honours the law's order while doing what the law could only certify, which is to make clean.

The psalmist blesses the LORD who forgives all iniquities and heals all diseases. In the house at Capernaum the two are joined in one scene. The man is first forgiven and then healed, as the psalm taught Israel to expect of their God, and the crowd's glory to God is the response the psalm calls for.

God's self-description before Moses includes forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin. The scribes' principle that God alone can forgive rests on this passage. By pronouncing forgiveness and then healing, Jesus exercises the prerogative God had named as His own character.

The vision of one like a son of man who is given dominion and kingship over all peoples. Jesus' title for Himself in verse 24 draws its weight from here. The authority to forgive sins on earth is the first display of the dominion Daniel saw given from heaven.

Matthew's account of the same call and meal, which names the tax collector Matthew and records Jesus' command to learn what 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice' means. Reading the two together confirms that the call came with a challenge to the Pharisees about what God actually wants.

The same complaint, 'This man welcomes sinners and eats with them,' prompts the parable of the lost sheep. Jesus answers the Pharisees' grumbling by saying there is more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous. The feast at Levi's house is a small enactment of that joy.

God rejoices over His people as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride. When Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom in verse 34, He takes up this picture of the covenant relationship, so that His presence is the wedding the prophets promised.

In Gethsemane Jesus prays 'Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me. Yet not My will, but Yours be done.' The words echo the leper's plea and Jesus' reply, 'I am willing.' The will that cleanses the leper is the will that carries Him to the cross, and the two scenes interpret each other.

Paul's summary of the gospel: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. It is the same claim as Luke 5:32, put in the voice of a man who counts himself the worst of them. Levi the tax collector and Paul the persecutor are examples of the same grace.

The next two controversies, about the Sabbath, complete the block of five conflicts that begins at Luke 5:17. The opposition grows as the claims of Jesus grow, and the passage ends with the scribes and Pharisees discussing what to do to Him, so that the cost of the bridegroom's presence comes into view.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible begins with a good world and a people who were made for fellowship with God. Sin broke that fellowship, and the long middle of the story is the question of how a holy God can dwell with a sinful people. The tabernacle, the sacrifices, the laws of cleanness and the priesthood were the answer given in advance: a way to approach God that kept the holiness and the sinner at a distance. Luke 5 shows what happens when God Himself comes near. The one who is holy is the one who touches the unclean, who forgives the guilty and who sits at the table with the despised.

The chapter answers the questions that the Old Testament leaves open. How can anyone stand before a holy God? Peter's cry and the response show that the answer is not distance but mercy. Who can forgive sins? The scribes know that God alone can, and the answer is that God is present in the Son of Man. Where is the bridegroom whom the prophets promised? He is eating and drinking with sinners in Galilee.

It also sets up what follows in the Gospel and in Acts. The nets that tear and the boats that begin to sink prepare for the great harvest of the church. The calling of fishermen and a tax collector shows the kind of people who will be sent as witnesses, and Peter will be the first to preach on Pentecost. The conflict with the Pharisees that begins here continues until the cross, where the Son of Man uses His authority to forgive in the fullest way. The parables of the new cloth and the new wine anticipate the church's struggle over what to keep and what to leave behind, a struggle that Acts 15 takes up directly, when Peter says that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, Acts 15:11.

The cross is where all of this is paid for. Jesus can say 'Your sins are forgiven' because He will bear them. The touch that cleanses the leper is the beginning of the exchange that ends with Him taking our uncleanness and giving us His righteousness. Every sinner called in the Gospels is called on the credit of what He will do.

The new creation gathers the harvest. The bride is made ready and the marriage of the Lamb is celebrated, Revelation 19:7, and the multitude from every nation is brought in. The people who left their nets and their tax booths to follow Him are at the feast. The old garment and the old wineskins are gone, and the new wine, which has been poured out since the Spirit came, is drunk without end. The one who once said 'Follow Me' to a man at a tax booth is the one at the head of the table.

quiz.q: How did Simon Peter respond to the miraculous catch of fish?

options.text: He fell at Jesus' knees and confessed himself a sinful man.
options.note: In verse 8 the catch reveals Jesus' holiness and Simon's sin, driving him to his knees.

options.text: He was amazed and grateful for such a great haul.
options.note: He was astonished, but his deeper response was conviction of sin, not just gratitude for the fish.

options.text: He immediately asked Jesus for another miracle.
options.note: He did not seek more signs; he shrank back, aware of his unworthiness before Jesus.

options.text: He doubted that the catch had anything to do with Jesus.
options.note: The opposite: he saw Jesus as Lord and felt his own sinfulness in His presence.

quiz.q: What was remarkable about how Jesus healed the man covered with leprosy?

options.text: He reached out and touched the man, then declared Him clean, willingly bearing contact with the unclean.
options.note: Verse 13 shows Jesus touching the leper, a startling act of compassion and power.

options.text: He healed the man from a distance with a word.
options.note: Jesus did speak, but Luke stresses that He touched the untouchable man, which is the striking detail.

options.text: He sent the man to the priests to be healed there.
options.note: He sent the cleansed man to the priest as a testimony, but the healing came from Jesus' own touch and word.

options.text: He refused to go near the man because of his disease.
options.note: Far from refusing, Jesus deliberately reached out and touched him.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus forgive the paralytic's sins before healing him?

options.text: To show that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, proven by the visible healing.
options.note: Verse 24 states His purpose: the healing demonstrates His authority to forgive.

options.text: Because the man's paralysis was directly caused by a specific sin.
options.note: Sin and suffering are related since the fall, but Jesus' point was His authority to forgive, not a one-to-one link.

options.text: To avoid having to heal the man at all.
options.note: He did heal him; the forgiveness and the healing together displayed His authority.

options.text: Because forgiveness is a lesser thing than healing.
options.note: Forgiveness is the greater gift; the healing was given to prove His right to forgive.

quiz.q: Whom did Jesus say He came to call?

options.text: Sinners to repentance, not the righteous, like a doctor who comes for the sick.
options.note: Verses 31 and 32 give His mission: He came for sinners, not the self-righteous.

options.text: The tax collectors and outcasts of society.
options.note: He does call such people, but His words name a wider principle: all who know they are sinners in need.

options.text: Those who had already made themselves righteous.
options.note: The opposite of His words; He says He did not come to call the righteous.

options.text: Only the religious leaders who kept the law.
options.note: He was criticized by those leaders precisely for calling sinners instead.

quiz.q: What do the parables of the patch and the new wineskins teach?

options.text: The new life of the kingdom Jesus brings cannot be confined to the old forms; it calls for something new.
options.note: Verses 36 to 38 show the new wine bursting old skins, a picture of the kingdom's newness.

options.text: That old traditions should always be discarded as worthless.
options.note: The point is the incompatibility of new and old forms, not that everything old is worthless; the old prepared for the new.

options.text: That Jesus came merely to patch up the existing religious system.
options.note: The parables say the opposite: His kingdom is not a patch on the old garment.

options.text: That fasting and prayer no longer matter at all.
options.note: Jesus says His followers will fast when the bridegroom is taken; the parables are about newness, not abolishing devotion.

questions: Simon obeyed Jesus even when it made no sense to his experience: 'because You say so, I will let down the nets.' Where is Jesus asking you to trust His word over your own judgment?
The catch of fish made Simon aware of his sin, yet Jesus said, 'Do not be afraid.' How does meeting the holiness of Jesus and His grace together change the way you come to Him?
Jesus touched the leper no one else would touch. Is there an area of shame or uncleanness in your life you fear to bring to Him, forgetting that He is willing?
The paralytic's friends carried him to Jesus and would not give up. Who are you carrying to Jesus in prayer, and whose faith once carried you?

Levi left everything at the tax booth and followed at once, then threw a feast so his friends could meet Jesus. What would leaving everything to follow look like for you, and who would you want at that table?

translationNotes.note: The Lake of Gennesaret is another name for the Sea of Galilee, as the BSB footnote notes. Luke, writing for a wider audience, uses the term lake rather than the more traditional sea.

Leprosy in Scripture covers a range of serious skin diseases, not only the condition called leprosy today, as the BSB footnote explains with reference to Leviticus 13. Such a person was ceremonially unclean and cut off from the community, which makes Jesus' touch all the more striking.

The offering Moses prescribed for a cleansed leper is set out in Leviticus 14:1-32. Presenting it to the priest served as a testimony that a true cleansing had taken place, a public witness to what Jesus had done.

Son of Man is Jesus' favored self-designation, drawing on Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man is given authority and everlasting dominion. Here Jesus claims that authority extends to forgiving sins on earth, which the scribes rightly regard as God's prerogative alone.
